metadata.note: The lesson names no assigned reading. Reading questions rest on the primary documents it cites (BIP 174, BIP 67, BIP 327, Electrum FAQ, Sparrow quick start), fetched 14 Nov 2026; BIP 174 was read only to its first 100,000 characters. Coverage: q1-q8 give one question to each visible check, worked example, practice, answers and review slide; q9-q14 cover the rule, witness, what-shows, key-order, Taproot and server slides.

questions.question_stem: A real mainnet spend has one input from a 62-character bc1q address. Output 1 pays a single-key address and output 2 returns the larger amount to the paying address. What is the best call on the change?
questions.correct_answer: Output 2 is the change, Moderate: it returns to the input's own address, one strong clue, and a single input rules out a CoinJoin.
incorrect_answers: Output 2 is the change, High: the same address and the same output type are two independent clues that point to one single, shared wallet.
Output 1 is the change, Moderate: a wallet's change normally goes to a single-key address, and the other amount is round.
No call can be made: a 2-of-3 wallet may pay itself, so an output back to the paying address says nothing about change.
questions.explanation: The change returns to the very address that paid, which is one strong clue; one input rules out a CoinJoin. A matching type is not a second clue, because an output to the same address always has the same type, so the call is Moderate, not High.
questions.lesson_block: A real 2-of-3 spend, before the theory
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: A real 2-of-3 spend, before the theory

questions.question_stem: An agent asks whether an unspent 3... output is a 2-of-3 multi-sig. What can the analyst say?
questions.correct_answer: Not yet: it shows only a script hash.
incorrect_answers: Yes: 3... is the P2SH form of multi-sig.
No: 3... outputs lock to a single key.
Yes: the address encodes its key count.
questions.explanation: Until it is spent, a 3... output is a hash of a script. It may be multi-sig, nested SegWit or any other script, so the type cannot be told. The rule is revealed only when the output is spent.
questions.lesson_block: Check: which wrapper is this output?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Check: which wrapper is this output?

questions.question_stem: A P2WSH 2-of-3 spend's witness is an empty item, two signatures, then a script listing keys K1, K2 and K3. A student writes that K3 did not sign. What is the best response?
questions.correct_answer: The explorer does not say. Signatures follow key order, so K1+K2, K1+K3 and K2+K3 all fit; only checking each signature against each key settles it.
incorrect_answers: Correct: signatures follow key order, so the two signatures listed in order are K1's and K2's, and K3 was left out of the set of signers.
Correct only if K3 is listed last, because an explorer keeps the keys sorted and so the first two signatures belong to K1 and K2 alone.
Unfounded, but the empty first item stands for the skipped key, so the dummy shows that exactly one of the keys stayed out of the spend.
questions.explanation: Any pair of the three keys signs in key order, so the order alone rules out no pair. The explorer does not label signatures; a node settles it by checking each signature against each key.
questions.lesson_block: Check: which key did not sign, and who signed?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Check: which key did not sign, and who signed?

questions.question_stem: An agent asks whether the real 2-of-3 spend was made with Electrum, given that its three keys run 02..., 03..., 02... in the script. What does the chain support?
questions.correct_answer: It names no program. Unsorted keys rule out a sortedmulti descriptor like Bitcoin Core's tutorial, but many programs build this script.
incorrect_answers: Electrum, because it is the lightweight program that builds P2WSH 2-of-3 scripts and leaves its mark in the witness script.
Bitcoin Core, because its 2-of-3 tutorial builds a P2WSH script and no other open-source program makes a script of that shape in practice.
A hardware wallet, because the unsorted key order shows that each key was added from its own device at setup, as is the usual way.
questions.explanation: The chain shows a script type and a transaction, never a program's name. Unsorted keys rule out one setup, sortedmulti, and name none; wallet habits are leads to check, not a name.
questions.lesson_block: Check: can you tell which software built it?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Check: can you tell which software built it?

questions.question_stem: Two signers have each run walletprocesspsbt on their own machines, and the PSBT has been combined and finalized. What is on chain before sendrawtransaction?
questions.correct_answer: None of the spend: still off chain.
incorrect_answers: The unsigned spend is in the mempool.
One signature, relayed to the nodes.
The signed witness, once it is merged.
questions.explanation: In the worked 2-of-3, only the last step, sendrawtransaction, puts the spend on the network. A PSBT that is never broadcast leaves no trace on chain.
questions.lesson_block: A PSBT carries a half-signed spend
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: A PSBT carries a half-signed spend

questions.question_stem: A second spend has one input from a 62-character bc1q address and a four-item witness: an empty item, two signature-sized items, then a script decoding as OP_PUSHNUM_2, three keys, OP_PUSHNUM_3, OP_CHECKMULTISIG. What is the reading?
questions.correct_answer: A P2WSH 2-of-3 multi-sig input with two signatures, since two items sit between the dummy and the script.
incorrect_answers: A P2WSH 3-of-3 multi-sig input with three signatures, since the script lists three keys, all needed.
A P2SH-P2WSH 2-of-3 multi-sig input with two signatures, since the last item is a witness program in the scriptSig.
A P2WSH 2-of-2 multi-sig input with two signatures, since two signatures appear and the third key is a backup.
questions.explanation: A 62-character bc1q input is P2WSH. The decoded last item gives 2-of-3, and the two items between the empty dummy and the script are the signatures.
questions.lesson_block: Practice: read a second real 2-of-3 spend
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Practice: read a second real 2-of-3 spend

questions.question_stem: In the second spend, an un-round amount goes to a new bc1q address of the input's type and 0.3 BTC goes to a single-key address. Why is the change call Moderate rather than High?
questions.correct_answer: Two weaker clues agree: the change has the input's script type and an un-round amount where 0.3 is round, but a careful wallet can defeat both clues.
incorrect_answers: Only one clue applies, since the change went to a new address instead of back to the payer, and one strong clue gives Moderate, as before.
The explorer cannot say which two keys signed, and that uncertainty about the signers lowers every change call in the spend to Moderate.
Any spend that needs several signatures is Moderate, because the rule keeps a wallet's own outputs from being told apart by any explorer.
questions.explanation: The confidence word follows the clues. The input's type and an un-round amount agree, but a careful wallet can defeat both, so the call is Moderate. The case was Moderate too, for a different reason: one strong clue.
questions.lesson_block: Answers: the payment, the change, and how sure
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Answers: the payment, the change, and how sure

questions.question_stem: An analyst drafts: "Three keys, so three people hold this wallet, and the first key listed is the lead signer." Which correction fits the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Three keys do not show three people, since one person can hold all three, and the key order carries no rank at all.
incorrect_answers: Three keys do show three holders, but the first key is the lead signer only when the building wallet sorted the keys.
Three keys show three people only if all three signed, and the first key listed is the one that signed first.
Three keys show three holders if the public keys all differ, and key order follows the order each holder joined.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin Core's tutorial builds a 2-of-3 from three wallets in one node, so keys are not people. Wallets sort keys by their bytes or order them as they choose, so position shows nothing about roles.
questions.lesson_block: Review: read the rule, not the people
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Review: read the rule, not the people

questions.question_stem: In a spend of OP_2 <A> <B> <C> OP_3 OP_CHECKMULTISIG, what is the empty item before the signatures?
questions.correct_answer: A dummy the opcode takes and ignores.
incorrect_answers: A placeholder for the key that skipped.
A marker holding the threshold value m.
A stand-in for the redeem script itself.
questions.explanation: The first item is a dummy that OP_CHECKMULTISIG takes and ignores; since SegWit it must be the empty byte array. It is not a placeholder for a key or the threshold.
questions.lesson_block: The rule is written in the script
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: The rule is written in the script

questions.question_stem: A P2WSH multi-sig input's witness has five items: an empty item, three signatures, then the witness script. What does the script's opening number show?
questions.correct_answer: That m is 3, because a spend supplies m signatures after the empty item and then the script.
incorrect_answers: That n is 3, because the script lists three keys and only three signatures match here.
That m is 4, because the empty item counts as a signature slot, so four slots are filled.
That m is 2, because a 2-of-3 is the usual form and the spare third signature is never checked.
questions.explanation: The number before the keys is m, the minimum number of signatures that must match a key. A spend supplies m signatures, in key order, after the empty dummy.
questions.lesson_block: A spend's signatures follow the keys' order
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: A spend's signatures follow the keys' order

questions.question_stem: Which statement about the real 2-of-3 spend can an analyst write as a plain reading, with no confidence word?
questions.correct_answer: Two valid signatures met a 2-of-3 rule, and the script type, its three keys and its outputs are all shown on chain.
incorrect_answers: The three keys belong to three people, since each of the three public keys sits in the witness script on chain.
A company or custodian is behind the keys, since a 2-of-3 rule is the usual setup for a company's treasury.
The keys are kept on separate devices, since the witness shows that each key signed from its own machine.
questions.explanation: The chain shows m, n, the keys, that m valid signatures were given, the script type and the outputs. Who holds the keys, whether an organisation is behind them and where they are kept are not shown.
questions.lesson_block: What a multi-sig spend shows, and what not
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: What a multi-sig spend shows, and what not

questions.question_stem: A student sees the case's keys listed as 02..., 03..., 02... and writes that the first key is the lead signer. What does the lesson say about key order?
questions.correct_answer: Position follows how the building wallet ordered the keys, often by their bytes, so it shows nothing about roles.
incorrect_answers: Position follows who joined the wallet first, so the first key's holder leads whenever the keys run in sorted order.
Position follows signing priority, and the unsorted 02..., 03..., 02... order shows the lead signer was chosen.
Position follows each key's value, so keys starting 02... outrank the key starting 03... and the first leads.
questions.explanation: BIP 67 sorts keys by their bytes so one set gives one address. Position follows the keys' bytes or the wallet's choice, not the people; the case's own keys are not even sorted.
questions.lesson_block: Key order in the script carries no meaning
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Key order in the script carries no meaning

questions.question_stem: A bc1p spend reveals a script: <A> OP_CHECKSIG, <B> OP_CHECKSIGADD, <C> OP_CHECKSIGADD, OP_2 OP_NUMEQUAL. How is it read?
questions.correct_answer: A script-path 2-of-3: a signature count.
incorrect_answers: A MuSig2 key-path spend of one joint key.
A 3-of-3 multi-sig where every key signs.
OP_CHECKMULTISIG under other opcode names.
questions.explanation: In tapscript, m-of-n uses OP_CHECKSIGADD, which adds one to a count for each valid signature, and the count is compared with m. OP_CHECKMULTISIG is disabled there; a MuSig2 key path would reveal no script.
questions.lesson_block: Taproot multi-sig can look like one key
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Taproot multi-sig can look like one key

questions.question_stem: A subject uses Electrum on a public server. An agent asks who off chain might know this wallet's addresses. What is the best answer?
questions.correct_answer: The server operator, who can link the addresses it was asked about and sees the client's IP address; keys stay with the user.
incorrect_answers: No one, because Electrum never sends private keys to the servers, so nothing about the wallet leaves the program, now or later on.
The subject's internet provider, who reads the wallet's addresses from the traffic and ties them to the account holder.
The miner of the block, who sees the wallet's addresses when each spend is mined and ties them to its IP address.
questions.explanation: A lightweight wallet asks a server about its addresses, so the server can link them and see where the request came from. Private keys are not sent, but addresses and IP address are.
questions.lesson_block: Servers learn which addresses a wallet has
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Servers learn which addresses a wallet has

questions.question_stem: A signer on an air-gapped machine is handed a PSBT for a multi-sig spend. What does that file hold for the signer?
questions.correct_answer: The information necessary for a signer to produce signatures, so the file can be carried to the signer.
incorrect_answers: Only the unsigned spend, so the signer must fetch what it needs from a full node before it signs.
The other signers' private keys, so the signer can produce every signature itself from the file alone.
A broadcast-ready transaction, so the signer's only job is to send it on to the network at once, unsigned.
questions.explanation: The slide quotes BIP 174: a PSBT is a file holding the information necessary for a signer to produce signatures. It is passed between signers, and nothing reaches the chain until the last step.
questions.lesson_block: A PSBT carries a half-signed spend
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: A PSBT carries a half-signed spend
questions.specific_source_reading: BIP 174 (Chow), Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction Format: purpose, as quoted on the slide

questions.question_stem: A hardware wallet and an air-gapped laptop are two of the three signers of a multi-sig spend. How can each take part?
questions.correct_answer: Each runs the same signing step on its own machine, adds one signature, and never sees another signer's private key.
incorrect_answers: Each must be online to broadcast, since every signer sends its own signature to the network when it is done.
Each receives the other signers' private keys inside the file, so it can check their signatures before it signs.
Each signs only after the spend is on chain, since a PSBT is a record of a transaction that is already mined.
questions.explanation: The slide names air-gapped and hardware wallets among the signers a PSBT serves. Each signer works on its own machine, in any order, adds one signature and sees no one else's private key. Only the final step broadcasts.
questions.lesson_block: A PSBT carries a half-signed spend
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: A PSBT carries a half-signed spend
questions.specific_source_reading: BIP 174 (Chow), Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction Format: signers named on the slide

questions.question_stem: Why does BIP 67 sort the keys of a multi-sig script by their bytes?
questions.correct_answer: So one key set gives one address.
incorrect_answers: So the lowest key leads the signers.
So nodes can reject unsorted keys.
So cosigners can sign in any order.
questions.explanation: Without a standard order, n keys give many orderings and so many different addresses for one setup. Sorting gives one canonical script and address. The network cannot enforce it, because a P2SH address does not reveal its script.
questions.lesson_block: Key order in the script carries no meaning
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Key order in the script carries no meaning
questions.specific_source_reading: BIP 67 (Kerin), Deterministic Pay-to-script-hash multi-signature addresses through public key sorting: motivation

questions.question_stem: A team says its Taproot output was set up with MuSig2 over five keys, and a spend shows one key and one signature. What do the team's statement and BIP 327 support?
questions.correct_answer: All five keys had to sign, and the chain still shows one key and one signature, so it does not show how many signed.
incorrect_answers: Any three of the five keys could have signed, since MuSig2 is a threshold scheme the chain shows as one signature.
The spend shows all five keys, since MuSig2 lists each cosigner's key in a script path just as OP_CHECKSIGADD does so.
One key signed alone, since a single signature on chain means a single signer and a key path has no cosigners.
questions.explanation: BIP 327 calls MuSig2 an n-of-n scheme, not a threshold scheme: every signer takes part. Its output looks like a regular single-signer Taproot output, so a lone signature does not show a lone signer.
questions.lesson_block: Taproot multi-sig can look like one key
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Taproot multi-sig can look like one key
questions.specific_source_reading: BIP 327 (Nick, Ruffing, Seurin), MuSig2 for BIP340-compatible multi-signatures: n-of-n and what an observer sees

questions.question_stem: An Electrum wallet never sends private keys to its servers, yet a public server can still link its addresses. What does the Electrum FAQ suggest to stop that?
questions.correct_answer: Run your own Electrum server, so that no outside operator can see which addresses your wallet asks it about.
incorrect_answers: Keep the private keys on a hardware device, so the server can no longer tell which addresses are linked.
Use a VPN alone, since hiding the client's IP address also stops the server linking its addresses to you.
Create more addresses in the wallet, since a larger set of addresses hides which of them are the wallet's.
questions.explanation: The Electrum FAQ says the client never sends private keys, but it subscribes to its addresses, so a server can infer one owner and sees the client's IP address. Fast startup is traded for this exposure, and running your own server is the remedy.
questions.lesson_block: Servers learn which addresses a wallet has
questions.specific_source_lesson: 06-BF-multisig_and_wallet_software.qmd: Servers learn which addresses a wallet has

questions.question_stem: A Sparrow user with significant funds connects it to a public server. What does the Sparrow quick start say is at stake?
questions.correct_answer: Privacy, not funds: public key information is shared with whoever runs the public server it uses, not the coins.
incorrect_answers: Funds, because a public server holds the wallet's public key information and so can sign spends for the user too.
Neither, because a public server sees only addresses that are already public on the chain, so it learns nothing new.
Neither, because a public server sees only addresses already public on the chain, so it learns nothing new.
questions.explanation: The slide quotes the Sparrow quick start: on a public server the user is sharing public key information, and thus privacy, with whoever runs it. Sparrow can instead connect to a Bitcoin Core node or a private Electrum server.
